lesson.title: Mapping the Electron Address Book
lesson.summary: Electron configuration is the shorthand notation, like 1s2 2s2 2p4, that records exactly which subshells and orbitals an atom's electrons occupy, built from the shell, subshell, and orbital structure you already know.
lesson.body:
Once you know that electrons live in orbitals grouped into subshells grouped into shells, the natural next question is: for a specific atom, which orbitals are actually occupied? Electron configuration is the notation chemists use to answer that question precisely. A configuration like 1s2 2s2 2p4 is read subshell by subshell: the number before the letter is the principal quantum number n (the shell), the letter is the subshell type (s, p, d, or f), and the superscript is the number of electrons sitting in that subshell. Add up the superscripts and you get the atom's total electron count.

Writing a correct configuration is not guesswork; it follows from three rules working together, each of which gets its own full treatment soon. The Aufbau principle says electrons fill the lowest energy subshells first. The Pauli exclusion principle caps every individual orbital at two electrons with opposite spins, which is why an s subshell (one orbital) holds at most 2 electrons, a p subshell (three orbitals) holds at most 6, a d subshell (five orbitals) holds at most 10, and an f subshell (seven orbitals) holds at most 14. Hund's rule governs how electrons spread across the multiple orbitals within one subshell before any pairing happens. Electron configuration is simply the bookkeeping that results from applying all three rules to a specific number of electrons.

Take oxygen as a worked example. A neutral oxygen atom has atomic number 8, meaning 8 protons and, in the neutral atom, 8 electrons. Filling from the lowest energy subshell up: the first two electrons fill 1s, giving 1s2. The next two fill 2s, giving 2s2. That accounts for 4 electrons, leaving 4 more, all of which go into the 2p subshell, giving 2p4. The full configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p4, and checking the arithmetic, 2 plus 2 plus 4 equals 8, matching oxygen's atomic number exactly.

Configurations get longer as atoms get bigger, but the logic never changes. Sodium, atomic number 11, is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1: the first ten electrons fill 1s, 2s, and 2p completely (2 + 2 + 6 = 10), and the eleventh electron starts a new subshell, 3s, alone. Notice that the configuration also tells you something chemically important at a glance: sodium's single 3s electron, sitting by itself in the outermost shell, is exactly the electron that makes sodium so reactive and gives it a plus one charge when it forms compounds.

One wrinkle worth flagging now, because it will matter as soon as you reach the Aufbau principle in detail, is that subshells do not fill strictly in order of increasing n. The 4s subshell, for instance, fills before the 3d subshell, even though 3 is a smaller shell number than 4, because 4s happens to sit at slightly lower energy in a multi electron atom. Electron configuration is therefore not just a matter of counting up shells in order; it reflects the actual energy ordering of subshells, which is precisely what the next few concepts will explain and formalize.
